prompt: How does a Grignard reagent, RMgX, react with a carbonyl compound?

choices.text: Its R group adds as a carbanion nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon, giving an alkoxide ion
It donates a hydride ion to the carbonyl carbon, giving an alkoxide ion
choices.why: Hydride donation is what NaBH4 and LiAlH4 do. A Grignard reagent delivers a carbon group, R:−.

choices.text: Its magnesium atom bonds to the carbonyl carbon, giving an organomagnesium alcohol
choices.why: Magnesium is the positive end of the reagent. The nucleophilic R group is what bonds to the carbonyl carbon.

choices.text: Its R group adds as a cation to the carbonyl oxygen, giving an ether
choices.why: The R group is negatively polarized (R:− +MgX) and adds to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon.

explanation: Grignard reagents act as nucleophilic carbanions (:R−). Their addition to a carbonyl compound is analogous to hydride addition: the R group bonds to the carbonyl carbon, and the alkoxide intermediate is protonated by H3O+ in a second step.

prompt: Why does the Grignard reaction have no direct counterpart in biological chemistry?

choices.text: Organomagnesium compounds are too strongly basic to exist in water
Living organisms never form new carbon–carbon bonds
choices.why: They do. Addition of stabilized carbon nucleophiles to carbonyl compounds is the major way metabolic pathways form C–C bonds.

choices.text: Carbonyl compounds don't occur in living organisms at all
choices.why: Carbonyl compounds are common in cells; for example, NADPH reduces the ketone acetoacetyl ACP (Section 17.4).

choices.text: Grignard reagents are too weak as nucleophiles to add to C=O
choices.why: Grignard reagents are strong nucleophiles. The problem is that they are too basic to survive in water.

explanation: Grignard addition has no direct biological counterpart because organomagnesium compounds are too strongly basic to exist in an aqueous medium. It does have an indirect counterpart: stabilized carbon nucleophiles add to carbonyl compounds in almost all metabolic pathways to form C–C bonds.

prompt: What kinds of alcohols do Grignard reagents give with formaldehyde, with other aldehydes, and with ketones?

choices.text: Formaldehyde: primary; other aldehydes: secondary; ketones: tertiary
Formaldehyde: primary; other aldehydes: primary; ketones: secondary
choices.why: That is the pattern for hydride reduction. A Grignard reagent adds an R group, so each product has one more R group on the alcohol carbon.

choices.text: Formaldehyde: secondary; other aldehydes: secondary; ketones: tertiary
choices.why: Formaldehyde, H2C=O, has no R groups. Adding one R group gives RCH2OH, a primary alcohol.

choices.text: Formaldehyde: primary; other aldehydes: tertiary; ketones: tertiary
choices.why: An aldehyde carbon already has one R group; adding one more gives two, a secondary alcohol.

explanation: Grignard reagents react with formaldehyde, H2C=O, to give primary alcohols, with other aldehydes to give secondary alcohols, and with ketones to give tertiary alcohols. In each case the alcohol carbon gains one R group from the reagent.

prompt: What alcohol forms when cyclohexylmagnesium bromide reacts with formaldehyde in ether, followed by H3O+?

choices.why: The cyclohexyl group bonds to the formaldehyde carbon, so the product has one more carbon: a –CH2OH group on the ring.
This tertiary alcohol needs a ketone, cyclohexanone, plus CH3MgBr.
Cyclohexane would form if the Grignard reagent were protonated by an acidic hydrogen. Formaldehyde has none, and the reagent adds to its C=O.

explanation: Grignard reagents add to formaldehyde to give primary alcohols with one added carbon. Cyclohexylmagnesium bromide and formaldehyde, followed by H3O+ workup, give cyclohexylmethanol.

prompt: What alcohol forms when phenylmagnesium bromide reacts with 3-methylbutanal, (CH3)2CHCH2CHO, followed by H3O+?

choices.why: The Grignard reagent adds a phenyl group, not a hydrogen, so the product contains a phenyl ring.
After H3O+ workup the product is an alcohol: the alkoxide ion formed by addition is protonated.
An aldehyde gives a secondary alcohol, with the phenyl group and the –OH on the former carbonyl carbon. This tertiary alcohol has a different skeleton.

explanation: Grignard reagents add to aldehydes to give secondary alcohols. The phenyl group bonds to the carbonyl carbon of 3-methylbutanal, giving (CH3)2CHCH2CH(OH)C6H5, 3-methyl-1-phenyl-1-butanol.

prompt: What alcohol forms when ethylmagnesium bromide reacts with cyclohexanone, followed by H3O+?

choices.why: The Grignard reagent adds an ethyl group to the carbonyl carbon, not a hydrogen.
The ethyl group bonds to the carbonyl carbon, the same carbon that ends up carrying the –OH.
That primary alcohol comes from cyclohexylmagnesium bromide and formaldehyde.

explanation: Grignard reagents add to ketones to give tertiary alcohols. The ethyl group bonds to the carbonyl carbon of cyclohexanone, which also carries the –OH after workup: 1-ethylcyclohexanol (also Exercise 17.5.3: cyclohexanone + CH3CH2MgBr).

prompt: How many equivalents of a Grignard reagent are used up when an ester such as ethyl pentanoate is converted into a tertiary alcohol?
explanation: Two. Esters react with Grignard reagents to give tertiary alcohols in which two of the groups on the alcohol carbon come from the Grignard reagent, just as LiAlH4 reduction of an ester adds two hydrogens.

prompt: What forms when ethyl pentanoate, CH3CH2CH2CH2CO2CH2CH3, reacts with two equivalents of methylmagnesium bromide, followed by H3O+?

choices.why: The alkoxy part of an ethyl ester is released as ethanol, not methanol.
That is what LiAlH4 gives. A Grignard reagent adds methyl groups, not hydrogens.
Esters react with two equivalents of Grignard reagent, so the product is a tertiary alcohol, not a ketone.

explanation: Two methyl groups from CH3MgBr end up on the former carbonyl carbon, along with the butyl chain, giving (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH2CH2CH3, 2-methyl-2-hexanol (85% yield). The ethoxy group leaves as ethanol.

prompt: What happens when a carboxylic acid is treated directly with a Grignard reagent, RMgX?

choices.text: Its acidic hydrogen protonates the reagent, giving R–H and the acid's magnesium salt
The Grignard reagent adds twice to the carbonyl, giving a tertiary alcohol
choices.why: That's what esters do. The acid's carboxyl hydrogen reacts with the basic Grignard reagent instead.

choices.text: The Grignard reagent adds once to the carbonyl, giving a ketone
choices.why: Acids give ketones only after pretreatment with the turbo-Hauser base, i-Pr2NMgCl-LiCl.

choices.text: The carboxylic acid is reduced to a primary alcohol by the reagent
choices.why: Grignard reagents add carbon groups. Reducing an acid to a primary alcohol takes LiAlH4 (Section 17.4).

explanation: Carboxylic acids don't give addition products with Grignard reagents, because the acidic carboxyl hydrogen reacts with the basic Grignard reagent to yield a hydrocarbon and the magnesium salt of the acid.

prompt: A carboxylic acid is first treated with i-Pr2NMgCl-LiCl (the turbo-Hauser base) and then with a Grignard reagent. What kind of product forms?

choices.why: With the turbo-Hauser base the book shows the reaction stopping at a ketone. Esters are what give tertiary alcohols.
Primary alcohols come from reducing acids with LiAlH4, not from Grignard addition.

choices.text: A hydrocarbon and the magnesium salt of the acid, with no addition
choices.why: That happens without the turbo-Hauser base. The complex makes the carboxylate more electrophilic so the Grignard reagent can add.

explanation: Carboxylic acids react with Grignard reagents to give ketones if they are first treated with i-Pr2NMgCl-LiCl, the turbo-Hauser base, which forms a complex and increases the electrophilicity of the carboxylate anion.

prompt: Which of these organohalides can be converted into a Grignard reagent?

choices.why: Its acidic –OH hydrogen would react with the basic Grignard reagent as fast as it forms.
Its acidic carboxyl hydrogen would destroy the Grignard reagent as fast as it forms.
A compound that is both an alkyl halide and a ketone would react with itself.

explanation: Grignard reagents can't be prepared from organohalides that contain other reactive groups. Acidic O–H, N–H, S–H, and CO2H hydrogens protonate the reagent, and carbonyl groups such as ketones are attacked by it. Bromocyclohexane has no such group.

prompt: Why can't a Grignard reagent be prepared from a compound that is both an alkyl halide and a ketone?

choices.text: The Grignard reagent would react with the ketone in its own molecule
Ketones are acidic enough to protonate Grignard reagents
choices.why: The groups that protonate Grignard reagents are acidic O–H, N–H, S–H, and CO2H. A ketone's problem is that the reagent adds to it.

choices.text: Magnesium can't react with any organohalide that contains oxygen
choices.why: The oxygen itself isn't the issue. The carbonyl group is, because the new Grignard reagent would attack it.

choices.text: The carbonyl group makes the C–X bond too strong to react with magnesium
choices.why: The halide can react. The trouble is that the newly formed Grignard reagent would add to the C=O in the same molecule.

explanation: A Grignard reagent can't be prepared from an organohalide that contains another reactive functional group. A compound that is both an alkyl halide and a ketone would react with itself.

prompt: Which ketone + Grignard reagent combination gives 2-phenyl-2-butanol, C6H5C(OH)(CH3)CH2CH3, after H3O+ workup?

choices.why: This adds a second methyl group, giving C6H5C(OH)(CH3)2, with no ethyl group.
Acetone supplies two methyl groups, so the product is again C6H5C(OH)(CH3)2.
An aldehyde gives a secondary alcohol, C6H5CH(OH)CH2CH3, with no methyl on the alcohol carbon.

explanation: 2-Phenyl-2-butanol has a methyl, an ethyl, and a phenyl group on the alcohol carbon. One group comes from the Grignard reagent and the other two from the ketone, so ethylmagnesium bromide + acetophenone works (as do CH3MgBr + propiophenone and C6H5MgBr + 2-butanone; Worked Example 17.3).

prompt: 2-Phenyl-2-butanol has a methyl, an ethyl, and a phenyl group on its alcohol carbon. How many different ketone + Grignard reagent combinations can make it?
explanation: Any one of the three groups can come from the Grignard reagent, with the other two on the ketone: ethylmagnesium bromide + acetophenone, methylmagnesium bromide + propiophenone, and phenylmagnesium bromide + 2-butanone (Worked Example 17.3).

prompt: Which ester gives 2-methyl-2-pentanol, (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH2CH3, when treated with two equivalents of methylmagnesium bromide, followed by H3O+?

choices.why: Adding two methyl groups to a pentanoate ester gives 2-methyl-2-hexanol, one carbon too many.
This gives (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH3, 2-methyl-2-butanol, with an ethyl group instead of a propyl group.
This gives (CH3)3COH, 2-methyl-2-propanol.

explanation: 2-Methyl-2-pentanol has two methyl groups and a propyl group on its alcohol carbon. The two identical methyls can both come from CH3MgBr, so the ester must supply the propyl group on its carbonyl carbon: an ester of butanoic acid, such as methyl butanoate (Worked Example 17.4).

prompt: Which ketone + Grignard reagent combination gives 2-methyl-2-pentanol, (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH2CH3?

choices.why: This gives 3-methyl-3-pentanol, with two ethyl groups on the alcohol carbon.
This gives 2-methyl-2-butanol, which has an ethyl group rather than a propyl group.
An aldehyde gives a secondary alcohol, CH3CH(OH)CH2CH2CH3, 2-pentanol.

explanation: The alcohol carbon of 2-methyl-2-pentanol carries two methyl groups and a propyl group. Starting from a ketone, either propylmagnesium bromide + acetone or methylmagnesium bromide + 2-pentanone works (Worked Example 17.4).

prompt: What alcohol forms when methylmagnesium bromide adds to benzophenone (diphenyl ketone), followed by H3O+?

choices.why: That would be the reduction product. CH3MgBr adds a methyl group, not a hydrogen.
The methyl, both phenyls, and the –OH all end up on the former carbonyl carbon; this name puts the –OH on a different carbon.
After H3O+ workup the oxygen remains as an –OH group, so the product is an alcohol.

explanation: A Grignard reagent adds to a ketone to give a tertiary alcohol. The methyl group bonds to the carbonyl carbon of benzophenone, giving (C6H5)2C(OH)CH3, 1,1-diphenylethanol (Exercise 17.5.1).

prompt: How could you make 4-methyl-1-pentanol, (CH3)2CHCH2CH2CH2OH, by a Grignard reaction?

choices.why: This adds only one carbon to a four-carbon group, giving (CH3)2CHCH2CH2OH, 3-methyl-1-butanol.
An aldehyde other than formaldehyde gives a secondary alcohol, here 5-methyl-2-hexanol.
This gives the secondary alcohol (CH3)2CHCH2CH(OH)CH3, 4-methyl-2-pentanol.

explanation: 4-Methyl-1-pentanol is a primary alcohol, RCH2OH, so it comes from a Grignard reagent and formaldehyde. The R group must be the five-carbon isopentyl group: isopentylmagnesium bromide, (CH3)2CHCH2CH2MgBr, + formaldehyde (Exercise 17.5.2).

prompt: Which ester + Grignard reagent combination gives 3-methyl-3-pentanol, CH3CH2C(OH)(CH3)CH2CH3?

choices.text: Ethyl acetate, CH3CO2CH2CH3, + 2 equivalents of CH3CH2MgBr
Methyl propanoate, CH3CH2CO2CH3, + 2 equivalents of CH3MgBr
choices.why: Two methyls plus the ester's ethyl give 2-methyl-2-butanol.

choices.text: Ethyl propanoate, CH3CH2CO2CH2CH3, + 2 equivalents of CH3CH2MgBr
choices.why: Two ethyls plus the ester's ethyl give three ethyl groups: 3-ethyl-3-pentanol.

choices.text: Methyl butanoate, CH3CH2CH2CO2CH3, + 2 equivalents of CH3MgBr
choices.why: Two methyls plus the ester's propyl give 2-methyl-2-pentanol.

explanation: 3-Methyl-3-pentanol has two ethyl groups and one methyl group on its alcohol carbon. With an ester, the two identical groups come from the Grignard reagent and the third from the ester's carbonyl side: an alkyl acetate with two equivalents of ethylmagnesium bromide (Exercise 17.5.2).

prompt: Ethyl pentanoate and two equivalents of CH3MgBr give 2-methyl-2-hexanol in 85% yield. How many moles of 2-methyl-2-hexanol would 0.400 mol of ethyl pentanoate give?
explanation: 0.400 mol × 0.85 = 0.34 mol. Each mole of ester uses two moles of CH3MgBr and gives one mole of the tertiary alcohol, plus ethanol.
